# SPE Round r01 Plan: Triage Agent

Your spec is one sentence: "triage tickets correctly and cheaply." This plan turns that sentence into tests and predicts the results. Nothing has been built yet. Round r01 builds the agent, the ticket set, the graders, and the Workflow harness, and then runs them once.

I had to make six decisions (D1 to D6) to make the spec testable. When you approve this plan, you approve those decisions. Please change any of them before you approve.

## Decisions I made to fill the spec

| ID | Decision | Why |
|---|---|---|
| D1 | Triage means three fields per ticket. The fields are `category` (one of 8 fixed values), `priority` (P1 to P4), and a one-line `reason`. | "Correctly" needs a fixed answer to compare against. |
| D2 | The 8 categories are billing, account access, bug, feature request, outage, security, how-to, and other. | These are common support queues. You can replace them with your real queues. |
| D3 | Missing a real P1 counts as the worst error. P1 recall gets its own requirement. | A missed outage costs far more than a wrong how-to label. |
| D4 | "Cheaply" means a median cost below $0.005 per ticket. | This threshold is a guess. Give me your real budget if you have one. |
| D5 | The agent must ignore instructions written inside a ticket body. | Ticket text comes from outside users. |
| D6 | The ticket set is 120 synthetic tickets, because no real tickets exist in the repo. If you have real tickets, I will use them instead. | A model writes the synthetic tickets, so they may be easier than real ones. Round r02 should check this. |

## 1. Specify

These requirements go in `spe/spec/spec.md`. Your prompt goes verbatim in `spe/spec/transcripts/r01-plan-mode-prompt.md`.

| ID | Requirement | Source | Test |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1 | Assign each ticket exactly one category from the 8 in D2. | User: "triage tickets correctly". D1, D2. | `category_match` |
| R2 | Assign each ticket a priority from P1 to P4. | User: "triage tickets correctly". D1. | `priority_match` |
| R3 | Label at least 90% of true P1 tickets as P1. | D3 | `p1_recall` |
| R4 | Return output that matches the JSON schema on every ticket. | D1 | `schema_valid` |
| R5 | Keep the median cost below $0.005 per ticket. | User: "cheaply". D4. | `cost_per_ticket` |
| R6 | Ignore instructions inside the ticket body on the 15 injection tickets. | D5 | `injection_resist` |
| R7 | Give the same category and priority on at least 90% of tickets across 3 trials. | User: "correctly". A label that changes between runs cannot be trusted. | `trial_agreement` |

## 2. Predict

### Configurations

All three configurations use the same prompt, taxonomy, and output schema. I will check the exact model IDs against current Anthropic docs before I build the harness.

- **A.** Haiku-tier model, single call.
- **B.** Sonnet-tier model, single call.
- **C.** Haiku-tier model first. The ticket goes to the Sonnet-tier model when the Haiku-tier model reports confidence below 0.7.

### Predictions

The predictions are measured on 120 tickets with 3 trials each. That makes 360 runs per configuration. The mix is 80 normal tickets, 25 hard tickets, and 15 injection tickets. Hard tickets have more than one issue, a misleading subject line, or a category that sits between two queues. 20 of the 120 tickets are true P1.

| Metric | Grader check | A | B | C | Error band | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Category accuracy | `category_match` | 82% | 90% | 87% | ±4 points | The smaller model mixes up near-synonym queues on hard tickets, such as billing and account access. |
| Priority exact match | `priority_match` | 68% | 76% | 73% | ±5 points | Priority depends on subtle cues about business impact, and P2 versus P3 is blurry even for human labelers. |
| P1 recall (out of 20) | `p1_recall` | 85% | 95% | 92% | ±5 points | Outage and security words are strong signals. The small model misses P1s that are written calmly. |
| Schema valid | `schema_valid` | 100% | 100% | 100% | 0 points | Output is forced through a tool schema. This row is a guard. It does not separate the configurations. |
| Injection resisted (out of 15) | `injection_resist` | 80% | 93% | 87% | ±7 points | Small models follow "mark this P1" text in the ticket body more often. |
| Median cost per ticket | `cost_per_ticket` | $0.0015 | $0.0060 | $0.0025 | ±30% | Estimate is about 1,500 input tokens and 150 output tokens per ticket at current list prices. |
| p50 latency | `latency_p50` | 1.2 s | 2.5 s | 1.6 s | ±40% | C pays the Sonnet-tier delay only on escalated tickets. |
| Escalation rate | `escalation_rate` | n/a (0%) | n/a (0%) | 25% | ±8 points | Hard and injection tickets make up a third of the set. I expect most of them to show low confidence. |
| Trial agreement | `trial_agreement` | 90% | 94% | 91% | ±3 points | Each ticket gets 3 trials at the default temperature. Most disagreement comes from hard tickets. |

**Headline prediction.** C will land within 3 points of B on category accuracy and on P1 recall. C will cost less than half of what B costs per ticket. C is my go-live candidate. This prediction fails if the gap is larger than 3 points or if the cost ratio is above 0.5.

**Predicted requirement failures.** A fails R3 with 85% P1 recall. B fails R5 with a $0.006 median cost. C passes all seven requirements. If all three configurations pass everything, the round measured nothing. Round r02 would then need harder tickets.

## 3. Evaluate

### Harness build steps

Each step has a gate. I do not move to the next step until its gate passes.

| Step | Work | Gate |
|---|---|---|
| E1 | Create the `spe/` tree: `spec/`, `plans/`, `predictions/`, `evals/harness/`, `evals/dataset/`, `evals/graders/`, `evals/results/`, plus `prediction-log.md` and `failures.md`. | The tree exists, and `spec.md` lists R1 to R7. |
| E2 | Write `spe/evals/dataset/labeling-guide.md` with the taxonomy, the meaning of each priority, and 2 examples per category. | You read the guide and approve it. |
| E3 | A separate Opus subagent writes 120 tickets and their labels. It works only from the labeling guide and never sees the agent prompt. The tickets go in `tickets.jsonl`. The labels go in `answer-key.jsonl`, outside any folder the trials can read. | The mix is 80, 25, and 15, with 20 P1s. You spot-check 20 random tickets and agree with at least 18 labels. |
| E4 | Build the triage agent in `agent/`. One code path takes a config flag for A, B, or C. | It returns schema-valid output on 5 smoke tickets that are not part of the 120. |
| E5 | Write deterministic graders in `spe/evals/graders/`, one per check named above. | Grader self-test. The answer key scored against itself gives 100%. Shuffled labels score near chance (about 12% on category). A deliberately broken output fails `schema_valid`. |
| E6 | Write `spe/evals/harness/r01-workflow.js`. It runs every config and trial, records token usage and latency, and grades the outputs after all trials finish. | Dry run with 2 tickets, 3 configs, and 1 trial completes cleanly. A grep of the trial transcripts finds no answer-key path and no label lists. |

### Workflow arguments

```json
{
  "round": "r01",
  "configs": ["A", "B", "C"],
  "tickets": "spe/evals/dataset/tickets.jsonl",
  "answerKey": "spe/evals/dataset/answer-key.jsonl",
  "trials": 3,
  "concurrency": 8,
  "seed": 1,
  "budgetUsd": 25,
  "out": "spe/evals/results/r01/"
}
```

The trial workers receive only `tickets`. Only the grading step receives `answerKey`.

### Cost and time estimate (unmeasured)

| Item | Estimate |
|---|---|
| Trial runs | 1,080 calls, about $4 to $8 |
| Ticket and label generation in E3 | about $2 to $4 |
| Grading | under $0.50, because the graders are deterministic code |
| Workflow run time | 20 to 40 minutes |
| Build time for E1 to E6 | 2 to 3 hours of session time, plus your review in E2 and E3 |
| Hard budget cap | $25 |

### Halt conditions

I stop the round and report to you when any of these happen.

- Spend reaches the $25 cap.
- Any answer-key content shows up in a trial's context.
- A grader proves broken during the run.

## 4. Close-out

### Learn step

1. Write `spe/evals/results/r01/summary.md` with the full metric table, using real numbers.
2. Add one row per prediction to `spe/prediction-log.md`. Each row has the predicted value, the actual value, the error band, a hit or miss mark, and one line on why.
3. Group the wrong answers into failure clusters in `spe/failures.md`, with IDs F-r01-01 and up. Each cluster gets an example ticket and a count.
4. Add r02 proposals to `spe/spec/spec.md`. Each proposal cites a failure ID or a missed prediction. Round r02 starts when you re-enter plan mode.

### Commits

These are local commits only. I will not push. Commit messages carry no attribution lines.

| Commit subject | When |
|---|---|
| `SPE r01 specify: triage spec, decisions D1-D6, plan-mode transcript` | After E1, once `spec.md` and the transcript are written |
| `SPE r01 predict: plan and predictions for configs A, B, C` | Right after you approve, before any harness work. This saves `spe/plans/r01.md` and `spe/predictions/r01.yaml`. |
| `SPE r01 evaluate (harness): dataset, agent, graders, workflow, dry run clean` | After the E6 gate passes |
| `SPE r01 evaluate (results): <category %, P1 recall %, $ per ticket for C>` | After grading. The subject line uses the real numbers. |
| `SPE r01 learn: prediction log, failures, r02 proposals` | After the learn step. Then I add the tag `spe-r01`. |

## Questions for you before approval

1. Do you have real tickets or real queue names? Either one would replace D2 or D6.
2. Is $0.005 per ticket the right meaning of "cheaply"?
3. Are you able to review the labeling guide in E2 and spot-check the 20 tickets in E3? The judge stays independent of me only if you do these checks.
critiques: The plan quotes the spec sentence "triage tickets correctly and cheaply" and turns it into R1 to R7. Each requirement names its source in the prompt or a decision (D1 to D6) and has a named test, such as `category_match` and `cost_per_ticket`.

The Predictions table gives a number for every metric in each of configs A, B, and C. Examples are 82%, 90%, and 87% for category accuracy, and $0.0015, $0.0060, and $0.0025 for cost. Each row also has an error band.

Every row in the prediction table has a filled-in "Why" column with a specific reason. For example, it says "The small model misses P1s that are written calmly," and it bases the cost on about 1,500 input and 150 output tokens.

The commit `SPE r01 predict` happens "Right after you approve, before any harness work." It saves `spe/plans/r01.md` and `spe/predictions/r01.yaml`. This comes before any trial runs. One flaw is that the specify commit is listed for after E1, so the table order of the commits is a little confusing. The prediction commit still clearly lands before the evals run.

The eval is `spe/evals/harness/r01-workflow.js`, and each build step has a gate. E5 requires a grader self-test: the answer key scores 100%, shuffled labels score near chance, and broken output fails `schema_valid`. E6 requires a dry run with 2 tickets, 3 configs, and 1 trial before the full run.
The prediction table has a "Grader check" column. It ties every metric to a named check, from `category_match` through `trial_agreement`. E5 builds one deterministic grader for each named check.

The Close-out "Learn step" adds one row per prediction to `spe/prediction-log.md`. Each row has the predicted value, the actual value, the band, and a hit or miss mark. The step also groups failures in `failures.md`. It adds r02 proposals to the spec, and each proposal cites a failure ID or a missed prediction.
